units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Thrusting her back .
Don’t hold me, mother. Don’t hold me—I’ll kill him!
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Gerald!
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Let me go, I say!
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Stop, Gerald, stop! He is your own father!
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: GERALD clutches his mother’s hands and looks into her face .
She sinks slowly on the ground in shame .
HESTER steals towards the door .
LORD ILLINGWORTH frowns and bites his lip .
After a time GERALD raises his mother up , puts his arm round her , and leads her from the room .
FOURTH ACT
Sitting-room at Mrs. Arbuthnot’s .
Large open French window at back , looking on to garden .
Doors R.C. and L.C.
GERALD ARBUTHNOT writing at table .
Enter ALICE R.C. followed by LADY HUNSTANTON and MRS. ALLONBY.
Lady Hunstanton and Mrs. Allonby.
units.name: ALICE

units.text: Exit L.C.
Good morning, Gerald.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Rising .
Good morning, Lady Hunstanton. Good morning, Mrs. Allonby.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Sitting down .
We came to inquire for your dear mother, Gerald. I hope she is better?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: My mother has not come down yet, Lady Hunstanton.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Ah, I am afraid the heat was too much for her last night. I think there must have been thunder in the air. Or perhaps it was the music. Music makes one feel so romantic—at least it always gets on one’s nerves.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: It’s the same thing, nowadays.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: I am so glad I don’t know what you mean, dear. I am afraid you mean something wrong. Ah, I see you’re examining Mrs. Arbuthnot’s pretty room. Isn’t it nice and old-fashioned?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Surveying the room through her lorgnette .
It looks quite the happy English home.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: That’s just the word, dear; that just describes it. One feels your mother’s good influence in everything she has about her, Gerald.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Lord Illingworth says that all influence is bad, but that a good influence is the worst in the world.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: When Lord Illingworth knows Mrs. Arbuthnot better he will change his mind. I must certainly bring him here.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I should like to see Lord Illingworth in a happy English home.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: It would do him a great deal of good, dear. Most women in London, nowadays, seem to furnish their rooms with nothing but orchids, foreigners, and French novels. But here we have the room of a sweet saint. Fresh natural flowers, books that don’t shock one, pictures that one can look at without blushing.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: But I like blushing.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Well, there is a good deal to be said for blushing, if one can do it at the proper moment. Poor dear Hunstanton used to tell me I didn’t blush nearly often enough. But then he was so very particular. He wouldn’t let me know any of his men friends, except those who were over seventy, like poor Lord Ashton: who afterwards, by the way, was brought into the Divorce Court. A most unfortunate case.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I delight in men over seventy. They always offer one the devotion of a lifetime. I think seventy an ideal age for a man.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: She is quite incorrigible, Gerald, isn’t she? By-the-by, Gerald, I hope your dear mother will come and see me more often now. You and Lord Illingworth start almost immediately, don’t you?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I have given up my intention of being Lord Illingworth’s secretary.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Surely not, Gerald! It would be most unwise of you. What reason can you have?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I don’t think I should be suitable for the post.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I wish Lord Illingworth would ask me to be his secretary. But he says I am not serious enough.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear, you really mustn’t talk like that in this house. Mrs. Arbuthnot doesn’t know anything about the wicked society in which we all live. She won’t go into it. She is far too good. I consider it was a great honour her coming to me last night. It gave quite an atmosphere of respectability to the party.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Ah, that must have been what you thought was thunder in the air.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear, how can you say that? There is no resemblance between the two things at all. But really, Gerald, what do you mean by not being suitable?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Lord Illingworth’s views of life and mine are too different.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: But, my dear Gerald, at your age you shouldn’t have any views of life. They are quite out of place. You must be guided by others in this matter. Lord Illingworth has made you the most flattering offer, and travelling with him you would see the world—as much of it, at least, as one should look at—under the best auspices possible, and stay with all the right people, which is so important at this solemn moment in your career.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I don’t want to see the world: I’ve seen enough of it.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I hope you don’t think you have exhausted life, Mr. Arbuthnot. When a man says that, one knows that life has exhausted him.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: I don’t wish to leave my mother.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Now, Gerald, that is pure laziness on your part. Not leave your mother! If I were your mother I would insist on your going.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON
